forces: Flute, solo violin, obbligato harpsichord, strings and continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord
intro: This is the third movement, Allegro, of Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050, a fugue in a gigue rhythm in which the solo violin enters first, followed by the flute and harpsichord. The whole opening section returns at the end.

sections.label: A · Fugue subject in violin, flute and harpsichord
sections.mNote: The soloists play the fugue subject before the strings enter.

sections.label: B · Triplets in B minor
sections.mNote: The soloists play the dance through minor keys.

sections.label: A′ · Violin restates opening theme, D major
sections.mNote: The D major opening returns in full.

cues.title: Opening entries, solo violin
cues.text: The solo violin begins with a dotted figure followed by a run of triplets. The flute enters next, then the harpsichord. The movement is in two beats to the bar, and the three parts start to overlap.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, III, bars 1–10, in the Mutopia edition: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=548.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Middle section in B minor
cues.text: After the close in D major, the middle section begins in B minor at bar 79, with the solo violin marked piano. The violin continues its triplets, and the same short figures now pass through minor keys. The harpsichord plays more running passages of its own.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, III, from bar 79; the solo violin is marked piano. Mutopia edition, music ID 548.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Violinist at Weimar, 1703
cues.text: In 1703 Bach played violin in Duke Johann Ernst III’s private orchestra at Weimar. He stayed for about half a year before he became an organist in Arnstadt.

cues.title: Harpsichord solo, bars 164–176
cues.text: The flute, violins, viola and bass instruments stop. For thirteen bars (bars 164–176 in the Mutopia edition) the harpsichord plays alone, its two hands exchanging running figures. It is the longest passage in the movement for the harpsichord without the other instruments.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), III, printed pp. 158–159: every staff but the harpsichord’s rests for thirteen bars (bars 164–176 of the Mutopia edition, music ID 548).
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First publication, 1852
cues.text: In 1852, more than a century after Bach’s death, C. F. Peters published the Fifth Brandenburg Concerto. It was performed at the Leipzig Gewandhaus the following year. The score used here descends from Wilhelm Rust’s edition of 1871.
cues.evidence: Publication and performance history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5. Mutopia identifies the Bach-Gesellschaft edition as its source.

cues.title: Return of the opening section
cues.text: The opening returns in D major, beginning with the solo violin. The flute and harpsichord follow in their original order. Bach repeats the whole outer section, and the strings again enter after the soloists.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, III, bar 233 onwards: written-out return of bars 1–78. Mutopia edition, music ID 548.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Music of the Bach Family, 2008
cues.text: The Advent Chamber Orchestra played this concerto last in a programme called Music of the Bach Family, given on 10 and 17 February 2008. Just before it, the orchestra’s flautist Constance Schoepflin played the flute concerto in G, Wq 169, by Bach’s son Carl Philipp Emanuel.
cues.evidence: The Advent Chamber Orchestra’s printed programme, February 10th & 17th 2008: Brandenburg No. 6, C. P. E. Bach’s flute concerto in G (Wq 169), then Brandenburg No. 5. https://www.ibiblio.org/pandora/vorbis/chamber_orchestra/MAR-08/readme.html

transitions.title: Triplets turn to B minor
transitions.from: A · Fugue subject in violin, flute and harpsichord
transitions.how: The outer section closes on D major. The violin then begins broken-chord triplets in B minor, marked piano. The two-beat metre continues unchanged, and the middle section develops the soloists’ figures through a succession of new keys.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, III, bars 77–89; Mutopia edition, music ID 548.

transitions.title: Solo violin begins the reprise
transitions.to: A′ · Violin restates opening theme, D major
transitions.how: The middle section ends with a cadence, and the solo violin restores the opening D major subject. Flute and harpsichord follow with their answering entries, and then the accompanying strings return. The short dotted figure and its triplets are heard again from the start of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, III, bars 232–242: cadence and written-out return. Mutopia edition, music ID 548.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050 — Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871)
source.locator: III. Allegro, printed pp. 152–164: solo violin begins, flute answers, then the harpsichord enters, left hand before right. Ripieno strings join later. The opening music returns in full at bar 233.

timeline.note: The solo violin begins alone with the dotted subject.
The flute answers the violin, and the two soloists continue together.
The harpsichord’s left hand enters with the subject; the right hand answers two bars later.
The viola begins the subject, followed by the ripieno violin. Cello and violone reinforce the bass.
The middle section begins in B minor. Solo exchanges alternate with passages for the full group.
The solo violin restarts the opening subject in D major.
The flute answers the violin again, repeating the opening exchange.
The harpsichord returns with its left-hand and right-hand entries.
The ripieno strings return in turn. The repeated opening section leads to the D-major close.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
